claim: Any language recognized by a linear RNN (LRNN) over the rationals lies in PNC1, meaning LRNNs can be simulated by log-depth arithmetic circuits (Theorem 3, Section 4).
LRNNs require only O(log n log* n) depth NC circuits, an O(log* n) overhead beyond the O(log n) depth of transformers/TC0 circuits (Corollary 5, Section 4).

Log-precision nonlinear RNNs can solve sorted deterministic graph connectivity, an L-complete problem, requiring Omega(log^2 n) depth and revealing a fundamental parallelization barrier absent in LRNNs (Theorem 2, Section 3.2).
Poly-precision nonlinear RNNs can express P-complete problems under FO reductions, implying no efficient parallel algorithm exists for them unless P=NC (Corollary 2, Section 3.1).
DPLR-based LRNN architectures such as RWKV-7 and DeltaNet can solve the PNC1-complete iterated 3x3 matrix multiplication problem using only 4 layers (Theorem 5, Section 5.1).

Experiments show nonlinear RNNs generalize on the L-complete graph connectivity task while transformers and Mamba fail to solve it, matching the theoretical complexity separation (Figure 2, Section 6).

For linear least-squares problems, subsampled natural gradient descent (SNGD) is shown to be directly equivalent to the regularized Kaczmarz method, and SPRING is equivalent to the Nesterov-accelerated regularized Kaczmarz (ARK) method (Theorem 1).
SNGD converges at rate (1-α)^t where α=λ_min(P̄), while SPRING converges at rate O((1-√(α/β))^t), giving up to a square-root improvement in iteration complexity over SNGD (Theorem 1).
For general quadratic losses, SNGD requires the regularization parameter λ to exceed a threshold λ0 to guarantee convergence, and can diverge if regularization is insufficient (Proposition 3).

Under an assumption that the regularized projector P̄ shares an eigenbasis with J^T J, SNGD provably outperforms SGD by a factor of k^β when the spectrum of the Jacobian decays polynomially (Theorem 4).

A unified algorithm (Algorithm 1) captures both SNGD (momentum μ=0) and SPRING (μ∈(0,1)) as momentum-based updates using subsampled Jacobians, enabling single-minibatch convergence guarantees of any batch size.
Analysis of SPRING's convergence for general (non-least-squares) quadratic losses is left open as Conjecture 7, despite numerical experiments showing large empirical performance gains over SNGD.

mmBERT is pretrained on 3 trillion tokens split across three phases: 2.3T tokens pre-training, 600B tokens mid-training for context extension, and 100B tokens in a decay phase (Section 3).
Cascading Annealed Language Learning expands language coverage across training phases from 60 to 110 to 1,833 languages, with temperature sampling decreasing from 0.7 to 0.5 to 0.3 (Section 3.2).
An inverse mask ratio schedule lowers the masking rate from 30% in pre-training to 15% in mid-training to 5% in the decay phase (Section 3.3).
On GLUE, mmBERT Base scores 86.3 average versus 83.3 for XLM-R Base, and mmBERT Small scores 84.7 versus 78.3 for Multilingual MiniLM (Table 2).
On XTREME, mmBERT Base averages 72.8 versus 70.4 for XLM-R, and on MTEB Multilingual, mmBERT Base averages 54.1 versus 52.4 for XLM-R (Table 3, Table 5).
Adding low-resource languages during the decay phase yields a 68% relative increase (12.1 absolute F1 points) on Tigray despite only 100B decay-phase tokens (Figure 2).
